scope: Read-only review of current Cloudflare documentation, official source, and installed SDK code. No deployment or live benchmark call.

findings.conclusion: Cloudflare manages hosted Worker connections. There is no documented per-Worker TCP pool size, idle timeout, socket reuse, or outbound HTTP version control in the Fetch API.
details: The Workers Node http.Agent is a stub; it does not supply its own connection pool or keep-alive control.
Connection headers are not used by the Workers Node HTTP wrapper. Adding Connection: keep-alive does not add a pool.

findings.conclusion: The installed worker-rs Fetch API calls the same Worker global fetch as JavaScript. It does not create a separate native Rust HTTP client.

local_proof.description: Fetch request adapter obtains WorkerGlobalScope from js_sys::global and calls fetch_with_request_and_init.
Foundation signed range request uses Fetch::Request(request).send().

findings.conclusion: worker-rs env.bucket returns the native JS R2Bucket binding. The owner resolution index already uses this API.

local_proof.description: Bucket has native binding type R2Bucket.
Wasm bindings call JS R2Bucket methods.
Owner resolution bucket uses env.bucket with BZ_RESOLUTION as the default binding name.

findings.conclusion: Current official guidance uses R2 bindings within the same account and the S3 API for cross-account access. Service bindings also require the target Worker in the caller account.

local_proof.description: R2 binding schema has no per-binding account_id and rejects additional properties. Its remote field is for local development.

details: Changing the wrapper language does not remove the owner/Foundation account boundary.
No Foundation Worker was deployed. No archive or index object was copied or moved for this review.

findings.conclusion: The current signed S3 path does not force connection close, create a custom client pool, or choose an HTTP version.

local_proof.description: signed_get uses the common S3 signed request builder.
Request headers contain SigV4 authentication fields and optional Range; no Connection close header.
request_with_headers creates a Worker GET Request with supplied headers.

details: Creating a new Request object does not prove that a new TCP or TLS connection is opened.

findings.conclusion: Fetch keepalive is not an available pool control. Reviewed workerd source leaves it unsupported and has a shared pooled HTTP/1.1 client.
limits: Open-source workerd settings are not proof of the hosted Workers egress pool configuration.
The local workerd version differs from the reviewed main commit.
A local reuse test does not prove production connection reuse.
The negotiated protocol on our hosted Worker-to-R2 S3 requests was not measured. HTTP/2 use is not claimed.

measurement_limits: Client TTFB includes the path to the Worker and the work before the first response byte. It does not isolate a TLS handshake.
The signed S3 response-header wait does not separate DNS, TCP/TLS setup or reuse, Cloudflare routing, R2 gateway/service work, backend queueing, or storage wait.
The source S3 collector CF-Ray location does not identify the physical R2 storage location. That location remains unknown.
Object GET and HEAD counters measure API operations, not physical disk reads.
No direct production socket-reuse trace or successful stack CPU profile was captured by this review.
safe_actions: Keep native R2 bindings for owner-account data and ordinary Worker fetch for Foundation cross-account S3 reads.
Keep a stable S3 endpoint and complete successful response bodies. Explicitly cancel rejected bodies when safe; do not drain an unbounded incorrect response.
Keep request I/O inside handlers. Do not retain global live fetch promises, response streams, or sockets as a connection pool.
Do not add per-request warmup HEAD calls or Node Agent wrappers as an unmeasured keep-alive fix.
Measure response-cache and archive-cache behavior separately from connection reuse before a further change.
